title: What the pandit reads
hook: the pandit reads and argues, but has he understood

segments.voice: Yesterday, Oankar made all: Brahma, the mountains, the ages and the Vedas, all traced back to the One. Your line was from the one. What did you trace back three steps? Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

A book highlighted in yellow, page after page. Margins full of notes. Somebody can quote chapter and verse, win every argument at the table, and still lose their temper at the waiter five minutes later. Reading is one thing. Being changed by what you read is another. The Oankar knows this gap well. It was answered, tradition says, to a pandit, a man of books, who read and explained sacred texts. And the poem keeps turning to him with a simple question: you've read it, but have you understood? Today: what the pandit reads.
screen: `PAGES HIGHLIGHTED IN YELLOW.` → `QUOTING ISN'T BEING CHANGED.` → `HAVE YOU UNDERSTOOD?`

segments.voice: The Oankar has a refrain, the line Sikhs call the rahao, the pause, where the poem stops to say what it's about. In paraphrase: listen, pandit, why write about the world's tangles? Write the Name of the Lord, as the Gurmukh does. Notice the verb. Not stop writing. Write something else. The pandit is a man of the pen, and Nanak hands the pen back to him, pointed in a new direction. Elsewhere in the poem, in paraphrase: reading and reading, the pandit argues his case, but he doesn't know the treasure that is inside him. That's the gap from the hook. A person can master the words of a book and never meet the One the book is about. Now, it would be easy to hear this as a story about someone else's priest. Sikh teaching doesn't leave it there. Guru Nanak says the same thing to every reader, and Sikh teachers turn it on their own reading of the Guru Granth Sahib. In the Asa di Var he puts it with a striking picture. In paraphrase: you could read cartloads of books, whole caravans of them, read through every month and every year of your life. Only one thing is counted; the rest is the noise of ego. The one thing is the Name, understood and lived. So the question in the Oankar isn't really for a pandit at a temple long ago. It's for anyone holding a book, or a phone, today. How much did I read? is an easy question. What did it change? is the hard one. Read and understand.
screen: `THE RAHAO: WHY WRITE THE TANGLES?` · `HE HANDS THE PEN BACK.` · `CARTLOADS OF BOOKS, ONE THING COUNTS.` · `WHAT DID IT CHANGE?` · then, large: `READ AND UNDERSTAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: understand one thing you've read. Think back over what you've read lately: a verse, an article, a line from a book, even a sentence from this path. Choose just one. Say it to yourself slowly. Then ask three plain questions. What does it actually say? What does it ask of me? Where, this week, would it make a difference? Don't hunt for something clever. Stay with the one line until it feels less like information and more like something you know. If you pray, you can ask for understanding. If you don't, let the line settle. The bell holds the time.
What the pandit reads. In the Oankar, the reader who argues but hasn't met what's inside him; the refrain hands him the pen to write the Name. Today's word.
Your line: read and understand. Today, read less than usual, and keep one line long enough to let it change one thing you do. Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of vichar, reflection on Gurbani, alongside reading it; study circles and katha, explanations of the hymns in the gurdwara, help listeners understand what is read.

original.note: O pandit: how the Oankar's refrain addresses him, listen, pandit.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poem criticizing priests of another religion.
what it means: a warning to anyone who reads: reading without understanding misses the treasure inside.
what a scholar hears: the rahao tells the pandit to write the Name; the Asa di Var says the same to all readers: one thing counts.

Editor: the hook's 'whose whole life was reading, copying and explaining sacred books' (unsourced, and 'copying' unsupported) became 'a man of books, who read and explained sacred texts'; the blanket claim 'Sikhs apply it to their own reading' became 'Sikh teachers turn it on their own reading', in the teach and the myth item.
